name: Sam Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Sam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and nothing you say will be tied to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a site carpenter for a contractor that builds schools and community buildings. Right now it's a new primary school, so I'm doing the roof structure, then the internal walls, door frames and the timber cladding outside. I start at seven, do the toolbox talk, then it's head down till break. I like building something kids will use for fifty years, that feels worth getting up for.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who do you spend your days with?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I've got an apprentice, Kofi, he's 18 and keen, and I'm responsible for him most days. Ana, my girlfriend, works in a bakery, and on Saturdays I coach the under-12s at the football club. I've got about four months saved. I use the AI chatbot now and then to check a building rule or help Kofi understand his college work, but mostly I learn from the older lads, same as I always have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's go through five pictures of the future. The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say no surprise, there's no app for hanging a door. I'd tell Kofi he picked the right trade. Online I'd maybe share something funny about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it just means I keep working and building up. I want to be a supervisor in a few years, marry Ana, buy a place. Hard work gets you there, and that doesn't change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going on the school job and the next one. Keep putting two hundred a month away. Maybe start the supervisor course next year, since the company pays for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's how I expected things to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Kofi picked the right trade. What would you tell him to focus on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting his hands right first, cutting to a line, measuring twice. Then learning to read drawings properly. The rest comes with time on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the AI chatbot any more than now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a bit for paperwork, the method statements and risk forms. But I'd still want Kofi learning from people. You can't learn to feel a straight edge from a screen.

S0.say: I'd say no surprise, there's no app for hanging a door, and tell my apprentice he picked the right trade.
S0.think: It means I keep working and building up toward supervisor, marriage and a home. Hard work gets you there, and that doesn't change.
S0.do: Keeps working on the school build and saves two hundred a month. Plans to start the company-paid supervisor course next year.
S0.quote: You can't learn to feel a straight edge from a screen.
S0.fieldNote: Sam believes in steady effort and learning from older workers. He takes his apprentice's training seriously. He uses AI a little but values hands-on learning more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is normal, every trade's had it. My grandad saw power tools come in and he was fine. I'd tell the lads to get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's mostly paperwork and planning that changes, and maybe some of the cutting goes to factories. A good carpenter who turns up on time will still have work. I'd be fine, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn whatever new tools the company starts using, once I'd seen them work on a site. I'd make sure Kofi learns them too. And I'd do the supervisor course, because supervisors deal with the new stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. A bit curious, if anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe some of the older lads who won't touch a phone. But I'd help them, same as they helped me. That's how a site works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the company need fewer carpenters?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a few fewer. But they'd still need good ones, and I plan to be one of those. If you work hard you'll be all right, that's what I believe.

S1.say: I'd say change is normal and every trade has had it, like my grandad seeing power tools come in. I'd tell the lads to get on with it.
S1.think: Mostly paperwork and planning change, and some cutting moves to factories. A good carpenter who turns up on time will still have work, so I'd be fine.
S1.do: Learns new tools once he's seen them work on a site and makes sure his apprentice learns them too. Takes the supervisor course.
S1.quote: My grandad saw power tools come in and he was fine.
S1.fieldNote: His faith in hard work makes him relaxed about steady change. He'd wait to see tools proven, then learn them and pass them on. He thinks the older workers deserve help, not blame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shock and people need to pull together. I wouldn't say the government should pay everyone, I'd say firms should keep people on and find them work. At church I'd say we need to look after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be scared. Hard work doesn't count for much if a robot works harder for nothing. I'd be thinking about Ana, and about Kofi, who's only just started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save every penny I could and cut out the nice stuff, eating out and the holiday. I'd take on weekend jobs for people in the club and church, fences, decking, anything. If it got bad, we'd move in with my parents, they'd help, that's what family's for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, properly. I'd feel like the rules had changed halfway through the game.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You believe hard work pays off. Does this shake that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it does. I'd still work hard, I don't know any other way. But I'd be angry, because I've done everything right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Kofi?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stay with me as long as there's work, and learn everything. And keep a bit of money aside, even at 18. I'd feel like I'd let him down, telling him the trade was safe.

S2.say: I'd say it's a shock and people need to pull together. Firms should keep people on rather than the government paying everyone, and we should look after each other.
S2.think: I'd be scared, because hard work doesn't count for much if a robot works harder for nothing. I'd think about Ana and my apprentice.
S2.do: Saves every penny and cuts eating out and holidays. Takes weekend jobs for people from the football club and church, and would move in with his parents if things got bad.
S2.feel: Properly scared, like the rules changed halfway through the game.
S2.quote: I'd still work hard, I don't know any other way. But I'd be angry, because I've done everything right.
S2.fieldNote: The fast version shakes his core belief that effort pays. He'd still turn to work and family rather than the state. He feels responsible for having told his apprentice the trade was safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if you don't sit around. I'd tell the lads to start learning the new stuff now. I'd tell Kofi to get his qualifications done fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think the supervisor route is my best bet. Someone has to be in charge of a site, deal with the client and sign things off. But I'm honestly not sure that lasts either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the supervisor course this year, not next. I'd learn the planning software and the AI tools the managers use. I'd keep saving, maybe up to two fifty a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I'd have a plan, and that helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not sure the supervisor job lasts either. What then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd look at something with people, maybe coaching or youth work, since I already do the football. I'd find something. I'm not sitting at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the wedding change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, we'd still get married next year. But we might rent longer instead of buying. I don't want a big mortgage with five years on the clock.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if you don't sit around. I'd tell the lads to learn the new tools now and my apprentice to finish his qualifications fast.
S3.think: The supervisor route is my best bet, because someone has to run a site and sign things off. But I'm not sure that lasts either.
S3.do: Takes the supervisor course this year instead of next and learns the planning software and AI tools managers use. Raises savings to about two hundred and fifty a month and rents longer rather than buying.
S3.feel: Worried, but steadied by having a plan.
S3.quote: I don't want a big mortgage with five years on the clock.
S3.fieldNote: Five years pushes him to act now rather than wait for proof. He has a fallback idea in coaching or youth work, which comes from his life outside work. The wedding stays, but buying a home is delayed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, so no excuses. I'd tell people to learn, save and help each other. Same as I always say, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels fine for me. I'd be a supervisor for a good while, we'd buy a house, and I'd have time to see what comes next. It's the older lads and the ones who don't bother I'd worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the supervisor course next year as planned and keep saving. I'd marry Ana and we'd buy a small place in a couple of years. I'd learn the new tools as they turn up on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with a bit of worry about the end of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to be doing in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Running sites, coaching football, maybe with a kid of my own on the team. That's the dream. If the sites go, the football doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd worry about the ones who don't bother. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some lads don't want to learn anything new, and they'll blame everyone else when it comes. I'd help them if they asked, but you have to want it. Ten years is enough warning for anyone.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, so no excuses, and tell people to learn, save and help each other.
S4.think: Ten years feels fine for me: years as a supervisor, a house and time to see what comes next. I'd worry about older workers and those who don't bother.
S4.do: Takes the supervisor course next year as planned and keeps saving. Marries Ana, buys a small place in a couple of years and learns new tools as they appear on site.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, with some worry about the end.
S4.quote: If the sites go, the football doesn't.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, he returns to his original life plan with small additions. His traditional outlook shows in his view that people must want to help themselves. He sees coaching as a part of life no machine touches.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time to do anything right, and hard work stops counting. What would help is firms keeping people on and training them, and keeping apprenticeships so young lads like Kofi have a start. Family and church would do the rest.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what it means for the kids I coach. They're 11 and 12. What do I tell them to train for? I honestly don't know, and that bothers me more than my own job.

headlineQuote: I like building something kids will use for fifty years, that feels worth getting up for.
portrait: Sam Santos is a 27-year-old site carpenter building schools and community buildings, responsible for an 18-year-old apprentice and coaching under-12 football on Saturdays. He lives with his girlfriend Ana, a baker, has about four months saved and uses AI now and then. He believes hard work pays, so he's calm if AI fizzles or changes things steadily. AGI in two years shakes that belief and leaves him scared and angry, turning to savings, side jobs and family. With five or ten years he moves into supervising, and with ten his old plans of marriage and a house go ahead.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there'd be no time to do anything right and hard work would stop counting.
whatWouldHelp: Firms keeping people on and training them, and keeping apprenticeships so young people get a start, with family and church doing the rest.
